nodes.text: TinyML systems run ML inference under a milliwatt on MCU-class hardware, but no standardized, reproducible benchmark compares hardware/software solutions on accuracy, latency, and energy together.

Deploying advanced ML at this scale requires co-optimizing every layer of the stack; without a common, fair yardstick, the impact of any one optimization is hard to isolate, and direct comparison across solutions is difficult, slowing innovation.
A general MCU benchmark (CoreMark) and existing ML-inference benchmarks (MLMark, MLPerf Inference) already exist and measure related things.

CoreMark does not run real ML workloads; MLMark and MLPerf Inference run real ML workloads but need gigabytes of memory and (for MLPerf Inference) exclude MCUs, and MLMark does not measure power -- none jointly fits TinyML's accuracy+latency+energy, MCU-scale needs.

Can one benchmark suite fairly measure accuracy, latency, and energy for representative ML workloads on MCU-class hardware, while still letting a specific hardware or software contribution be demonstrated and directly compared against a common reference?
nodes.audience_note: Requires knowing what an MCU-class resource envelope is (N20) before this question is legible.

nodes.text: A modular reference-implementation design, combined with mandatory accuracy+latency+energy measurement and a closed/open division split, can let heterogeneous TinyML hardware and software submitters each demonstrate a distinct advantage while still supporting a fair, direct comparison.

MLPerf Tiny: four representative reference benchmarks (keyword spotting, visual wake words, image classification, anomaly detection), each pairing a dataset, an MCU-sized reference model, and a quality target set at a margin below the model's own measured accuracy, released with full open-source reference implementations and a runner that measures latency, energy, and accuracy under a fixed protocol.

A closed division fixes the dataset, model, and quality target (only post-training quantization allowed) so that hardware/software stacks can be compared head-to-head; an open division allows changing dataset, training, or model, without a mandatory accuracy bar, provided every deviation is documented.
nodes.audience_note: Requires PTQ vs. QAT and the closed/open idea (N21) before this is legible.

nodes.text: First real-world test of the design: solicit and score actual community submissions against the reference implementations in the v0.5 round (June 2021), transparently peer-reviewed by the submitter group and a review committee.

Five submissions arrived, spanning both divisions and five hardware/software categories: an ARM MCU, a RISC-V MCU, a Raspberry Pi 4 via a hardware-agnostic software toolchain, a dedicated neural-network accelerator, and an FPGA via a training-to-HLS workflow.

Across the five submissions, INT-8 was the most common numeric format, frameworks ranged from open interpreters to hardware-specific compilers, measured power spanned microwatts to watts, and no submission changed the training dataset.

This range of divisions, hardware classes, and software stacks, each demonstrating a different point in the deployment stack, is consistent with the modular design achieving its goal of accommodating TinyML's heterogeneity while the closed division kept results directly comparable.

An open, community-built, modular benchmark suite that jointly measures accuracy, latency, and energy for representative ML workloads on MCU-class hardware -- filling a gap left by CoreMark, MLMark, and MLPerf Inference -- and whose first real submission round shows it can accommodate the field's hardware and software diversity.
The evidence that the design 'works' comes from one round with five submissions, with no non-modular baseline suite to compare adoption against.
The reference accuracy/AUC figures behind each benchmark's quality-target margin are single measurements; no retraining or seed variance is reported.

Excluding feature extraction from the measured window keeps benchmarks comparable but risks a 'degenerate case' (defining most of the model as feature extraction); including it would, in this non-streaming protocol, run far more feature-extraction cycles than inference cycles per second of audio, over-counting that cost.
The closed division's reference architectures cover mainly FC and CNN layers; other families (e.g. RNNs) are reachable today only through the open division.

A suite with an easily extended edge (open division, modular components) but a fixed, comparable core (closed division) is positioned to keep tracking TinyML progress as the field's hardware and software diversity grows, and is already being reused as a standard task set.

Planned or needed extensions: new application-domain benchmarks alongside a stable long-term core subset; wider measurement scope covering pre-processing/streaming; broader closed-division architecture coverage (e.g. RNNs).
TinyML / MCU-class resource envelope: ML inference under a milliwatt of power, on devices with roughly two orders of magnitude less memory than smartphone-class ML, typically clocked 10-250 MHz.
nodes.audience_note: Needed before N01, N05, and N07.

nodes.text: Post-training quantization (PTQ, compressing an already-trained model's numeric precision) vs. quantization-aware training (QAT, retraining with quantization simulated); the closed division permits only PTQ, the open division also permits QAT/retraining.
nodes.audience_note: Needed before N08 and before Table 2's results are legible.

nodes.text: AUC-ROC as a threshold-free accuracy metric, used for the anomaly-detection benchmark because an anomaly score otherwise needs an arbitrary decision threshold.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: Modular reference implementations, a closed/open division split, and mandatory 3-metric measurement will let heterogeneous submitters each show a distinct advantage while keeping direct comparability.
experiment_chains.falsifier: Submissions arrive in only one division or one hardware class, or show no discernible distinct 'demonstrated' advantage each -- i.e. homogeneous uptake despite the suite being open for submission.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: A real, community-solicited submission round (rather than a synthetic stress test) is the only way to observe whether actual TinyML hardware/software providers use the suite's flexibility, and whether the closed division yields directly comparable results across differing hardware.
experiment_chains.next: Establishes that the design attracted and could score diverse submissions; the Discussion then asks what one round still cannot show (single-round evidence, unreplicated reference accuracies, and the two design tensions the authors flag in Section 8), which sets up the paper's limitations and future-work agenda.
